title: Offers, deadlines and return offers
objectives: Handle an offer with a deadline, compare offers, and turn an internship into a return offer.

screens.title: Two firms, one deadline
screens.prose: Firm A offers you an internship on day 0 and gives you 14 days to accept. Firm B, which you prefer, holds its final round on day 10 and decides by day 18.
screens.question: Drag Tell B to the day you should tell firm B about A's deadline.

hints.text: How much time would B need to move its process?
The earlier B hears, the more it can change.
Day 1: the day after the offer.

feedback.correct: Day 1: as soon as the offer is confirmed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Give B as many days as you can.

byKey.late: You waited. By then B has less time to bring its final forward, or none.
byKey.tell: Drag Tell B to the start of A's window.

explain.text: Tell B on day 1 or 2, while there are 12 or more days to work with. B may bring its final forward, or tell you it cannot. Waiting until day 10 or later leaves B no room.

screens.prose: Those are **offer moves**. About two weeks is a typical deadline (a careers adviser, eFinancialCareers, April 2004). That source is old; Quantt's UK guide (2026) reports one to two weeks.
screens.question: Put the moves in order. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: Thank firm A and confirm the deadline in writing
Tell firm B about the deadline and ask if it can speed up
If B cannot, ask A once for more time, with a reason
Decide, and answer A by the deadline
Say nothing to A and wait to be chased
lines.why: You went silent. An unanswered offer can simply be withdrawn.

hints.text: What fixes the clock first?
The deadline in writing comes before anything else.
Thank and confirm, tell B, ask A once if needed, decide.

feedback.correct: Thank, tell B, ask once, decide.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each move needs the one before it.

byKey.ghost: You kept the silence. Ignoring an offer risks losing it.
byKey.left-out: You left out a move that belongs. Only the silence goes.

explain.text: Thanking A and getting the deadline in writing fixes the clock. Telling B at once gives it the most time. An extension request comes after B's answer is known, so it can carry a reason.

screens.prose: B says it cannot decide before day 18. You ask A for more time. Day 0 was 2 March, so A's deadline is 16 March. Requests like this are often refused, so ask once, early and politely (eFinancialCareers, April 2004).
screens.question: Which email is best?

options.text: "Thank you again for the offer. I expect another decision on 20 March. Could I reply by 21 March?"
"I need until 23 March. Other firms are interested in me."
options.why: You demanded. A threat makes a refusal easier, not harder.

options.text: "Could I have a bit more time to think?"
options.why: You were vague. With no date or reason, the firm cannot say yes.

options.text: "I'm so sorry to ask, I know this is awkward, I feel terrible..."
options.why: You apologised at length. One polite line and a date are enough.

hints.text: What does a firm need to say yes?
A reason and one clear date.
Thanks, the reason, one date just after B decides.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the email that is easy to say yes to.

explain.text: The strong email thanks the firm, gives a reason and names one date. Firms often refuse, so a request that is easy to grant has the best chance. If A says no, you still decide by 16 March.

screens.prose: Comparing two offers, as reported. Pay figures are third-party reports and vary by firm and year. You used both in l2.

rows: £4,350 a week at one London trading firm
Bank summer analysts: about £65,000 a year, pro rata
Return rates: 70% to 80% at top trading firms, about 50% at banks

screens.question: Fill in firm A's pay for a 10-week internship.

hints.text: Pay for ten weeks is ten weekly payments.
The weekly figure is in row 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the weekly pay by 10.

byKey.r0c1: Check firm A's pay. Ten weeks is ten weekly payments: £4,350 × 10.

explain.text: £4,350 × 10 = £43,500, against £12,500 at the bank (l2). Pay matters, but if you want a full-time job, the return rate and the work matter more. Both pay figures are third-party reports, so treat them as rough.

screens.prose: You accepted Bank C's offer in writing on day 5. On day 9, firm A offers too.
screens.question: What does accepting C mean now?

options.text: Withdraw politely from every other process, A included
Keep the other processes open, just in case
options.why: You kept interviewing after accepting. Firms see that as bad faith.

options.text: Take A's offer and tell C you have changed your mind
options.why: You reneged. It burns the relationship with C, and at some universities the careers service's too.

options.text: Accept A as well and decide later
options.why: You accepted two offers. One of them will be broken.

hints.text: What did you promise C on day 5?
Accepting is a promise to turn up.
Withdraw from the rest.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Accepting is a promise.

explain.text: Accepting is a promise, so withdraw from the rest the same week. Reneging burns your relationship with the firm. At some universities it also harms the careers service's relationship with that firm.

screens.prose: In the internship. Return-offer decisions usually come in the last weeks (Quantt guides, 2026). A **return offer** is the full-time job offered at the end.
screens.question: Select all that apply: what is reported to count towards a return offer?

options.text: Ask questions early, then fewer as you learn
Own one project from start to finish
Write the project up clearly
Be the same person on day 50 as on day 1
Stay quiet until you are sure of yourself
options.why: You stayed quiet. Early questions are expected; silence looks like being stuck.

options.text: Join as many projects as you can
options.why: You spread yourself thin. One finished project is what is judged.

hints.text: What is judged in weeks 9 and 10?
The project, presented and written up.
Questions early, one project owned, a clear write-up, steady effort.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep what helps one project finish well.

explain.text: Return offers go to interns who learn fast, finish one project and explain it well. Consistency matters: day 50 is judged like day 1. Decisions come in the last weeks, so the write-up counts.

screens.prose: Firm A offers on day 0 with a 14-day deadline. You hope to hear from firm B, which you prefer.
screens.question: What should you do?

options.text: Tell B now, ask A for time once if needed, and decide by day 14
Accept A now to be safe, and renege if B says yes
options.why: You accepted to be safe.

options.text: Let A's deadline pass and wait to be chased
options.why: You ignored the deadline.

options.text: Decline A now, since you prefer B
options.why: You gave up a sure offer for a hope. Keep A until B decides or the deadline arrives.

hints.text: Which plan keeps a promise and the deadline?
Accepting is a promise; a deadline is real.
Tell B, ask A once, decide in time.

feedback.correct: Tell, ask once, decide in time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep both firms' trust.

byKey.safe: You accepted to be safe, planning to renege. Accepting is a promise, and breaking it burns the relationship.
byKey.ignore: You ignored the deadline, hoping to be chased. An unanswered offer can simply be withdrawn.
byKey.decline: You declined a real offer for a hoped-for one. You may end with neither.

explain.text: Both shortcuts break the offer's rules: accepting is a promise, and a deadline is real. The honest route has three moves: tell B, ask A once, decide in time. It keeps both firms' trust.

screens.prose: An edge case. It is March 2027. Nadia is preparing for summer 2028, and a small trading firm makes her a late offer for summer 2027.
screens.question: How should she weigh the offer?

options.text: Against her full plan: does a 2027 internship help her 2028 applications?
Against having nothing this summer, so accept at once
options.why: You compared it with nothing. Her real alternative is a summer of projects and preparation.

options.text: Refuse: it is not the cycle she is preparing for
options.why: You ruled it out by the calendar. An internship a year early is often strong 2028 evidence.

options.text: Accept on condition it moves to 2028
options.why: You assumed a deferral. Most offers are for one summer; ask, but do not count on it.

hints.text: What is her real alternative this summer?
Row 1: projects and preparation.
Compare with that plan, not with nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what she would do instead.

explain.text: The right comparison is her best plan, not an empty summer. A 2027 internship usually strengthens 2028 applications, so it is often a yes. She checks it does not clash with exams.

screens.prose: Another edge case. An offer letter reads: "conditional on the right to work in the Netherlands and a 2:1 or above".

rows: Right to work in the Netherlands

screens.question: What should Nadia do first?

options.text: Check the right to work at once, and ask the recruiter if unsure
Accept, and check the conditions in June
options.why: You put the condition off. If it fails in June, the place is gone and so are the others.

options.text: Worry only about the degree class
options.why: You checked the easy one. Her predicted First meets it; the work permit is the open question.

options.text: Ignore it: conditions are a formality
options.why: You assumed a formality. A right to work cannot be waved through.

hints.text: Which condition is still unknown?
Row 1 says "Not checked".
Check the right to work now.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the condition that is still unknown.

explain.text: A conditional offer falls away if the condition fails. Her grade looks safe; the right to work needs checking now. Ask the recruiter what help they give with permits before you accept.

screens.prose: Comparing pay used one rule. For an internship of $w$ weeks, $$\text{pay} = \text{weekly} \times w = \text{yearly} \times \frac{w}{52}$$ Compare offers over the same number of weeks.
screens.question: A bank pays £60,000 a year, pro rata, for a 9-week internship. What is the pay?

hints.text: What share of a year is 9 weeks?
Nine weeks is 9/52 of a year.

byKey.ten: You used 10 weeks. This internship is 9 weeks long.

explain.text: $60{,}000 \times \tfrac{9}{52} \approx \text{£}10{,}385$. As a check, a year's pay is about £1,154 a week, and nine of those make about £10,385. Always compare offers over the same number of weeks.

screens.prose: **Follow-up.** Firm B replies on day 2: "We can't move the final, but we can decide by day 12." A's deadline is still day 14. Pace: reply within a day.
screens.question: What do you do?

options.text: Thank B and wait for its answer on day 12; no extension needed
Ask A for an extension to day 21 anyway
options.why: You asked for time you do not need. Save requests for when they carry a reason.

options.text: Accept A now, to be safe
options.why: You took A before B could answer, though B will answer in time.

options.text: Decline A now
options.why: You gave up A before B has decided.

hints.text: Is day 12 before or after A's deadline?
Day 12 is two days before day 14.
Both answers arrive in time; no extension needed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare day 12 with A's deadline.

explain.text: Day 12 falls inside A's deadline, so both answers will be in hand by day 14. An unneeded extension request spends goodwill. Thank B, and plan to decide on day 12 or 13.

screens.prose: Return-offer arithmetic. In a weak year, one high-frequency firm reportedly made 29 return offers to 55 interns. Source: eFinancialCareers, November 2023, citing anonymous insiders.
screens.question: What was that year's return rate?

hints.text: Return offers over interns.
29 over 55.

feedback.correct: About 53%. You decide on an offer with a deadline in homework 3.

byKey.miss: You found the share without an offer: 26 of 55.
byKey.flip: You divided 55 by 29. Put the offers on top.

explain.text: $29 / 55 \approx 0.527$, about 53%, against about 80% reported for a strong year. The year is outside your control; your project, questions and write-up are not. You decide on an offer with a deadline in homework 3.

ideas: Thank the firm and confirm the deadline in writing. Tell other firms at once; ask for more time once, with a reason.
Compare offers over the same weeks, and weigh the return rate and the work beside the pay.
Accepting means withdrawing from the rest; a return offer comes from one project, owned and written up.
summary.trap: Accepting to be safe and reneging later, or ignoring a deadline in the hope of being chased.

quiz.question: An offer arrives on 3 May with a deadline of 13 May. Another firm's final round is on 9 May. When do you tell that firm?

options.text: On 3 or 4 May
On 9 May, at the final
options.why: You waited for the final. The firm then has four days to decide.

options.text: On 12 May, the day before
options.why: You left it to the last day. The firm cannot move that fast.

options.text: Never: offers are private
options.why: You kept it private. Telling them is normal and lets them speed up.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Give the other firm the most time.

explain.text: Telling the other firm at once gives it ten days to bring its decision forward. Firms expect this and often can.

quiz.question: An internship pays £3,200 a week for 12 weeks. What is the total?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the weekly pay by 12.

byKey.ten: You used 10 weeks. This internship is 12 weeks.

explain.text: $3{,}200 \times 12 = 38{,}400$. As a check, 10 weeks is £32,000 and 2 more add £6,400.

quiz.question: Select all that apply: which can an intern control in the return-offer decision?

options.text: Finishing one project well
A clear write-up
Asking questions early
Whether it is a strong year for the firm
options.why: You picked the firm's year. That is outside your control.

options.text: The size of the intern class
options.why: You picked the class size. The firm sets it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only what the intern decides.

explain.text: The firm's year and class size set the rate. Your project, write-up and questions set your place in it.

quiz.question: You accepted an offer last week. A firm you prefer now offers too. What do you do?

options.text: Keep your word, thank the second firm and decline
Take the second offer and tell the first firm
options.why: You reneged. It burns the relationship, and at some universities the careers service's too.

options.text: Hold both and decide in the summer
options.why: You held two offers. One promise will be broken.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Accepting is a promise.

explain.text: An accepted offer is a promise. Decline the second firm politely; you may meet it again next cycle.
